prompt:
You are an associate in the appellate litigation group at a mid-size New York law firm. A senior partner has asked you to prepare a comprehensive legal memorandum analyzing the New York Court of Appeals decision in Matter of P.C. v. Stony Brook University (2025 NY Slip Op 01566). The firm's client, a private university in New York, has expressed concerns about the potential impact of this decision on its own student disciplinary procedures and has requested guidance on how to structure its review panels and evidentiary standards in sexual misconduct proceedings to ensure judicial deference.

The attached document is the full Court of Appeals opinion in Matter of P.C. v. Stony Brook University, decided March 18, 2025. The opinion addresses the standard of review for university disciplinary determinations in CPLR article 78 proceedings, the substantial evidence standard as applied to student conduct findings, the role of respondent's silence at the hearing, and the presumption of non-responsibility under the university's Code of Student Responsibility.

Your memorandum must accomplish the following:

1. Identify and explain the procedural history of the case, including the original disciplinary charges, the Review Panel's determination, the administrative appeal, the Appellate Division's ruling, and the Court of Appeals' reversal.

2. Analyze the Court of Appeals' application of the substantial evidence standard, explaining how the Court evaluated the sufficiency of the evidence—including S.G.'s testimony, P.C.'s text messages, and the surveillance footage—and why it concluded the Review Panel's determination was supported.

3. Address the Court's treatment of P.C.'s decision to decline to answer questions at the hearing, including whether the Review Panel improperly drew adverse inferences from his silence and whether this implicated the presumption of non-responsibility.

4. Discuss the Appellate Division majority's reasoning and the dissent's position, identifying the key points of disagreement between them.

5. Provide practical guidance for the firm's university client, identifying specific procedural and evidentiary practices that would help ensure its disciplinary determinations receive judicial deference under the substantial evidence standard, based on the Court's analysis in this opinion.

The memorandum should be no more than 8 pages, single-spaced, with section headings for each major topic. Use standard legal citation format and cite to the opinion throughout.

sections.heading: I. Introduction and Issue Presented
required_content: Identification of the case and citation
Statement of the central legal issue regarding substantial evidence review of university disciplinary determinations
Brief description of the holding
paragraphs: This memorandum analyzes the New York Court of Appeals decision in Matter of P.C. v. Stony Brook University, 2025 NY Slip Op 01566 (March 18, 2025), and its implications for university student disciplinary proceedings in New York. The central question presented is whether a university disciplinary determination finding a student responsible for sexual misconduct is supported by substantial evidence under CPLR article 78 review, and the extent to which a respondent student's decision to decline to answer questions at the disciplinary hearing affects the evidentiary analysis.

The Court of Appeals held that the Review Panel's determination was supported by substantial evidence and reversed the Appellate Division's order that had annulled the determination and directed expungement. The decision clarifies the deferential standard of review applicable to university disciplinary findings and addresses the permissible scope of consideration of a respondent's silence in the evidentiary record.

sections.heading: II. Procedural History
required_content: September 2019 investigation commenced
Charges filed: sexual harassment, nonconsensual sexual contact, nonconsensual sexual intercourse/penetration
Definitions from Code of Student Responsibility § VII.C.6.a, b, c
Review Panel hearing with P.C. represented by counsel
Review Panel found P.C. responsible by preponderance of the evidence and imposed suspension
Administrative appeal upheld determination
CPLR article 78 proceeding filed
Appellate Division granted petition (221 AD3d 686, 2d Dept 2023)
Court of Appeals reversed, reinstating the determination
paragraphs: In September 2019, following a report that petitioner P.C. had engaged in behavior violating the University's sexual misconduct policy, Stony Brook University commenced an investigation. The other student involved, S.G., provided a written statement to the investigator. P.C. declined to meet with the University's investigator.

P.C. was subsequently charged with violating three provisions of the Code of Student Responsibility: sexual harassment (Code § VII.C.6.a), nonconsensual sexual contact (Code § VII.C.6.b), and nonconsensual sexual intercourse and/or penetration (Code § VII.C.6.c). The Notice of Charges alleged that P.C. "engaged in sexual contact with a female student while she was incapacitated due to alcohol and unable to give consent," including specific behaviors of choking S.G. during sexual intercourse in the woods and having sexual intercourse in S.G.'s vehicle.

A hearing was held before a Review Panel composed of faculty and staff members. P.C. was represented by counsel. S.G. testified and was cross-examined, with video surveillance footage showing the two walking together around campus played during cross-examination. P.C. provided an opening statement but declined to answer most questions on the advice of counsel, including whether he could identify actions or words by S.G. that constituted affirmative consent. Text messages between P.C. and a mutual friend were introduced into evidence, in which P.C. admitted having sex with S.G., stated "I made my choice, and I'm sorry, and I know I f***ed up," and acknowledged he "did something terrible."

The Review Panel found P.C. responsible by a preponderance of the evidence and imposed a suspension penalty. The Panel relied on S.G.'s testimony regarding unwelcome sexual advances, contact, and intercourse, as well as P.C.'s text messages. The Panel stated it had considered all available information and determined that, regardless of whether S.G. was incapacitated by alcohol, the evidence supported the conclusion of responsibility.

P.C. administratively appealed, arguing the violations were not established by a preponderance of the evidence and that the Panel improperly held his silence against him. The Appeals Committee found "no grounds upon which to alter the Review Panel's determination" and upheld the penalty, explaining that P.C.'s decision not to answer questions limited the evidence that could be considered.

Petitioner commenced a CPLR article 78 proceeding seeking to vacate the determination. Upon transfer from Supreme Court pursuant to CPLR 7804(g), a majority of the Appellate Division (221 AD3d 686, 2d Dept 2023) granted the petition, annulled the determination, dismissed the charges, and directed expungement. The majority found substantial evidence lacking, referencing S.G.'s written statement about earlier consensual activity, and found that reliance on P.C.'s silence violated the presumption of non-responsibility. Two Justices dissented. The Court of Appeals reversed the Appellate Division's order.

sections.heading: III. Substantial Evidence Analysis
required_content: Explanation of the substantial evidence standard in CPLR article 78 review
S.G.'s testimony about choking during sex and her brief unconsciousness in the car
P.C.'s text messages admitting sexual intercourse and stating he "f***ed up" and "did something terrible"
Surveillance footage and its limited relevance
The Review Panel's specific factual findings
Court's conclusion that the Panel's determination was supported
paragraphs: Under CPLR article 78, a disciplinary determination must be annulled if it is not supported by substantial evidence. The Court of Appeals applied this standard to the Review Panel's findings and concluded that the determination was supported by substantial evidence, warranting reversal of the Appellate Division.

The evidentiary record included several categories of proof. S.G. testified that during sexual intercourse, P.C. choked her aggressively, that she "felt like I couldn't breathe" and "tried to get his hands off my throat," that P.C. "wasn't budging," and that she subsequently blacked out. With respect to the sexual intercourse in her car, S.G. testified that she remembered "dreaming as if she were asleep," and when she woke up, she "remembered panicking" and asking P.C. if she had passed out, to which he initially said no but then acknowledged she was "only out for a moment." She testified she told her friends she "woke up and it was still happening. He didn't stop."

Additionally, text messages between P.C. and a mutual friend were introduced into evidence. In these messages, P.C. admitted having sex with S.G., stating "I made my choice, and I'm sorry, and I know I f***ed up, and I won't sugar coat that." He also acknowledged he "did something terrible" and explained his conduct by stating he "was drunk and horny and let my monkey brain have fun in the moment" and that "if I had been sober, I would've been thinking more straight and I wouldn't have hurt her nor broken your trust."

The Review Panel specifically found that the evidence supported the conclusion that P.C. engaged in unwelcome sexual advances, unwelcome sexual contact, and unwelcome sexual intercourse. Critically, the Panel stated that, regardless of whether S.G. was incapacitated by alcohol, the evidence supported responsibility for the charged misconduct. The Court of Appeals concluded that these findings were supported by substantial evidence, including S.G.'s testimony about the unwelcome choking and her brief unconsciousness during the car encounter, corroborated by P.C.'s own text message admissions.

sections.heading: IV. Treatment of Respondent's Silence and the Presumption of Non-Responsibility
required_content: P.C.'s decision to decline to answer questions at the hearing
The Appeals Committee's explanation regarding the effect of silence on the evidentiary record
The Appellate Division majority's concern about adverse inference from silence
The Court of Appeals' resolution of this issue
paragraphs: A significant issue in the case concerned P.C.'s decision to decline to answer most questions at the hearing on the advice of counsel, including whether he could identify actions or words by S.G. that constituted affirmative consent. The Review Panel and Appeals Committee addressed this silence, with the Appeals Committee explaining that while P.C. was permitted to decline to answer questions, the Panel was "constrained to consider only the evidence in the record" and that his silence "limited the evidence that could be considered."

The Appellate Division majority found that the University's reliance on P.C.'s silence violated the presumption of non-responsibility contained in the Code of Student Responsibility. This presumption effectively placed the burden of proof on the University to establish responsibility, and the majority viewed the consideration of P.C.'s decision not to testify as improperly shifting that burden.

The Court of Appeals' reversal implicitly addressed this issue by reinstating the determination. The Court's analysis focused on the affirmative evidence in the record—S.G.'s testimony and P.C.'s text messages—rather than relying on adverse inferences from silence. The Appeals Committee's characterization of the effect of silence was that it limited the record available for review rather than constituting an affirmative adverse inference. The Court of Appeals' conclusion that substantial evidence supported the determination, independent of any inference from silence, resolves the concern that the determination rested on an improper evidentiary basis.

sections.heading: V. Disagreement Between the Appellate Division Majority and Dissent
required_content: The Appellate Division majority's reasoning that substantial evidence was lacking
The majority's reference to S.G.'s written statement about earlier consensual activity
The majority's finding regarding improper reliance on P.C.'s silence
The dissent's position that the determination should be confirmed
Key points of disagreement
paragraphs: The Appellate Division split on the question of whether substantial evidence supported the Review Panel's determination. The majority granted the petition, annulled the determination, dismissed the charges, and directed the University to expunge the matter from petitioner's academic record (221 AD3d 686, 2d Dept 2023).

The majority deemed the only question to be whether substantial evidence supported the conclusion that S.G. did not otherwise consent to the sexual activity, since the Review Panel made no determination regarding incapacitation by alcohol. The majority found substantial evidence lacking, specifically referencing S.G.'s written statement that she consented to sexual activities earlier in the evening. The majority also found that reliance on P.C.'s decision not to answer questions violated the presumption of non-responsibility in the Code of Student Responsibility.

The two dissenting Justices would have confirmed the determination, denied the petition, and dismissed the proceeding. The dissent concluded that the determination that petitioner violated the Code of Student Responsibility was supported by substantial evidence. The fundamental disagreement between the majority and dissent centered on how to weigh the totality of the evidence, including S.G.'s testimony about unwelcome conduct and P.C.'s text message admissions against S.G.'s statements about earlier consensual activity, and whether consideration of P.C.'s silence constituted an improper adverse inference or a permissible acknowledgment of gaps in the evidentiary record.

sections.heading: VI. Practical Guidance for University Disciplinary Proceedings
required_content: Emphasize documented factual findings in the hearing record
Ensure disciplinary charges specifically identify the Code provisions violated with their text
Record all testimony and evidence with specificity
Obtain written admissions or contemporaneous communications where possible
Address the presumption of non-responsibility carefully in procedures and panel instructions
Frame the effect of respondent's silence as limiting the record rather than as adverse inference
Apply the preponderance of the evidence standard consistently
Document the Panel's reasoning and the specific evidence relied upon for each charge
paragraphs: Based on the Court of Appeals' analysis, the following practices would help ensure that university disciplinary determinations receive appropriate judicial deference:

First, the hearing record should contain detailed, specific factual findings. The Review Panel in P.C. identified the specific testimony and documentary evidence supporting each charged violation. University panels should similarly document the particular evidence supporting each finding of responsibility, including specific testimony quotes and exhibits.

Second, the Notice of Charges should set forth the full text of the Code provisions alleged to be violated, as was done in this case. This ensures the respondent has adequate notice and facilitates meaningful appellate review.

Third, universities should make all reasonable efforts to secure documentary and testimonial evidence. In P.C., the text messages in which P.C. admitted sexual intercourse and acknowledged wrongdoing were critical to the substantial evidence determination. Universities should advise investigators to seek and preserve contemporaneous communications between parties and witnesses.

Fourth, the presumption of non-responsibility and the burden of proof should be carefully addressed. The Appeals Committee's approach in P.C.—explaining that the respondent's silence limited the available evidence rather than creating an adverse inference—was ultimately upheld. University procedures should frame the effect of declining to answer questions in these terms, emphasizing that the institution retains the burden of proof at all times and that silence simply means the panel must decide based on the evidence before it.

Fifth, review panels should expressly state that they have considered all available information and should identify the standard of proof applied. The Review Panel's statement that it considered all available information and determined responsibility regardless of the intoxication issue was a sound approach that demonstrated careful, fact-specific analysis.

Sixth, universities should ensure that their appeal procedures and committees provide meaningful review while respecting the original panel's factual findings. The Appeals Committee in P.C. conducted an independent review of the evidence and articulated its reasoning, which supported the finding that the determination was neither arbitrary nor unsupported.

sections.heading: VII. Conclusion
required_content: Summary of the Court of Appeals' holding
Key takeaways for university disciplinary proceedings
Recommendation for client to review its procedures in light of this decision
paragraphs: The Court of Appeals' decision in Matter of P.C. v. Stony Brook University confirms that university disciplinary determinations in sexual misconduct cases will receive substantial judicial deference when supported by detailed factual findings and adequate evidentiary records. The reversal of the Appellate Division majority underscores that reviewing courts should not reweigh the evidence or substitute their judgment for that of the disciplinary panel when substantial evidence exists to support the determination.

The key takeaways for our client are: (1) build a robust evidentiary record at the hearing level; (2) document specific factual findings tied to each charged violation; (3) carefully frame the treatment of respondent silence; and (4) ensure the review panel articulates its reasoning and the standard of proof applied. We recommend that the client conduct a comprehensive review of its current disciplinary procedures and panel training materials in light of this decision to ensure alignment with the standards endorsed by the Court of Appeals.

# Seed Material: Matter of P.C. v. Stony Brook Univ.
Source: courtlistener
Identifier: cluster:10357504

Case Name: Matter of P.C. v. Stony Brook Univ.
Citation: 2025 NY Slip Op 01566
Court: ny
Date Filed: 2025-03-18
Judges: None

## Opinion Text
Matter of P.C. v Stony Brook Univ. ( 2025 NY Slip Op 01566 ) Matter of P.C. v Stony Brook Univ. 2025 NY Slip Op 01566 Decided on March 18, 2025 Court of Appeals Cannataro Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. This opinion is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. Decided on March 18, 2025 No. 25 [*1]In the Matter of P.C., Respondent, v Stony Brook University, et al., Appellants. Elizabeth A. Brody, for appellants. Alexander Klein, for respondent. CANNATARO, J. Petitioner, a student at respondent Stony Brook University (the University), commenced this CPLR article 78 proceeding challenging the determination that he violated the University's Code of Student Responsibility by committing sexual misconduct against another student. We hold that the determination at issue is supported by substantial evidence and therefore reverse the order of the Appellate Division. I. In September 2019, following a report indicating that petitioner, P.C., had engaged in behavior that violated the University's sexual misconduct policy, the University commenced an investigation. The other student involved, S.G., provided a written statement to the investigator in which she recounted the details of their encounter. P.C. declined to meet with the University's investigator. Following the investigation, P.C. was charged with violating three provisions of the Code of Student Responsibility relating to sexual misconduct, namely, sexual harassment, nonconsensual sexual contact and nonconsensual sexual intercourse and/or penetration. The Notice of Charges detailed the allegations lodged against P.C., that he "engaged in sexual contact with a female student while she was incapacitated due to alcohol and unable to give consent," and listed specific behaviors, including choking S.G. during sexual intercourse in the woods and having sexual intercourse in S.G.'s vehicle. The Notice also set forth in full the text of the Code provisions P.C. was alleged to have violated. As relevant here, the definition of sexual harassment encompasses unwelcome sexual [*2]advances and physical conduct of a sexual nature, including sexual violence (Code of Student Responsibility § VII.C.6.a). Nonconsensual sexual contact includes "any contact of a sexual nature which is unwanted or unwelcome" (Code of Student Responsibility § VII.C.6.b) and nonconsensual sexual intercourse is "any sexual penetration or intercourse that is unwanted or unwelcome" (Code of Student Responsibility § VII.C.6.c). II. A hearing was held before a Review Panel composed of faculty and staff members from the University. P.C. was represented by counsel. The University's investigator placed a summary of the investigation on the record and S.G. gave a statement consistent with her prior written statement. With respect to the choking allegation, S.G. testified that she had been "black[ing] out," but "became present in the moment because of how aggressive [P.C.] was being, how I felt like I couldn't breathe and tried to get his hands off my throat. He wasn't budging and I don't know what happen[ed] after that because I blacked out again." With respect to the sexual intercourse in her car, S.G. stated that she did not recall much of what happened, but remembered "dreaming as if [she] were asleep" and, when she "woke up," she "remember[ed] panicking, asking [P.C.] if I passed out" and that he initially said no, but then said she was "only out for a moment." She also recalled swiftly terminating the encounter, returning to her dorm and crying on the phone with her friends, telling them that she "woke up and it was still happening. He didn't stop." Video surveillance footage showing the two walking together around campus at various points in the evening was played during the cross examination of S.G. P.C. provided a brief opening statement denying that he engaged in sexual conduct with S.G. while she was incapacitated due to alcohol and unable to consent. He generally argued that S.G. was not credible, asserting that the surveillance footage showing the two walking together around campus at various points in the evening belied any claim of inability to consent due to incapacitation by alcohol. He also argued that the allegation that she was violently choked should not be believed, given that there were no marks on her neck. P.C. confirmed that he was familiar with the definition of affirmative consent set forth in the Code of Student Responsibility. P.C. then declined to answer most of the questions asked by the hearing officer on the advice of counsel, including whether he could identify actions or words by S.G. during the sexual interactions that constituted affirmative consent. No other testimony was taken, but text messages exchanged between P.C. and another individual—a mutual friend who had introduced P.C. and S.G. that evening and had elicited a promise from P.C. that he would not have sex with S.G.—were introduced into evidence. In the messages, P.C. admitted he had sex with S.G., stating "I made my choice, and I'm sorry, and I know I f***ed up, and I won't sugar coat that." P.C. also acknowledged that he "did something terrible, and I don't know how to say I'm sorry, but I am." In explaining why he had sex with S.G., he said "I was drunk and horny and let my monkey brain have fun in the moment despite the obvious long-term outcome. What I'm saying is that if I had been sober, I would've been thinking more straight and I wouldn't have hurt her nor broken your trust." The Review Panel found P.C. responsible for violating the charged provisions of the Code of Student Responsibility by a preponderance of the evidence at the hearing. In support of its determination, the Review Panel pointed to S.G.'s testimony that P.C. engaged in conduct that amounted to unwelcome sexual advances, unwelcome sexual contact and unwelcome sexual intercourse, primarily that S.G. did not want P.C. to choke her during sex and that he admitted to her that she was briefly unconscious while they were having sex in the car. The Panel also cited to P.C.'s text messages, in which he acknowledged engaging in sexual intercourse with the victim and stated that he "f***ed up." The Review Panel stated that it had considered all available information and determined that, regardless of whether S.G. was incapacitated by alcohol, the evidence supported the conclusion that P.C. was responsible for the charged misconduct. The Panel imposed a penalty of suspension from the University. P.C. administratively appealed the determination, arguing that the violations of the Code of Student Responsibility were not established by a preponderance of the evidence. Despite his acknowledgement that the Review Panel did not base its determination on the question of S.G.'s inability to consent due to intoxication, P.C. nonetheless devoted a significant portion of his argument to evidence that purportedly negated any claim that S.G. was incapacitated by alcohol. He further posited that the evidence introduced at the hearing was sufficient to establish affirmative consent, citing S.G.'s statements relating to their consensual sexual activity that night. Finally, he argued that the Review Panel improperly held his decision to remain silent against him and improperly referenced his inability or unwillingness to identify evidence establishing affirmative consent, in violation of the presumption of non-responsibility contained in the Student Code. The Appeals Committee found "no grounds upon which to alter the Review Panel's determination" and upheld the disciplinary penalty. The Committee rejected the argument that S.G. was not credible. In addition, the Committee found that the evidence supported the Review Panel's findings of responsibility on all three charges based on a preponderance of the evidence. The Committee explained that, although P.C. was permitted to decline to answer questions put to him at the hearing, the Review Panel was constrained to consider only the evidence in the record and that his decision not to answer questions limited the evidence that could be considered. III. Petitioner commenced this CPLR article 78 proceeding against respondents [FN1] seeking to vacate the Appeals Committee's determination, asserting that it lacked substantial evidence and that it was arbitrary and capricious and made pursuant to an error of law due to the University's failure to follow its own rules for disciplinary proceedings. In particular, he asserted that the University did not adhere to the standard requiring that misconduct be established by a preponderance of the evidence and that it failed to accord him a "presumption of innocence." [FN2] Upon transfer from Supreme Court pursuant to CPLR 7804 (g), a majority of the Appellate Division granted the petition, annulled the Appeals Committee's determination, dismissed the charges and directed the University to expunge the matter from petitioner's academic record ( 221 AD3d 686 [2d Dept 2023]). Since the University Review Panel made no determination that S.G. was unable to consent as a result of incapacitation caused by intoxication, the Court deemed the only question before it to be whether substantial evidence supported the conclusion that S.G. did not otherwise consent to the sexual activity. The majority determined that substantial evidence was lacking to support that conclusion, specifically referencing S.G.'s written statement that she consented to sexual activities earlier in the evening. In addition, the majority found that reliance on P.C.'s decision not to answer certain questions violated the presumption of non-responsibility contained in the Code of Student Responsibility. Two Justices dissented and would have confirmed the determination, denied the petition and dismissed the proceeding. ## Opinion Text
Matter of P.C. v Stony Brook Univ. ( 2025 NY Slip Op 01566 ) Matter of P.C. v Stony Brook Univ. 2025 NY Slip Op 01566 Decided on March 18, 2025 Court of Appeals Cannataro Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. This opinion is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. Decided on March 18, 2025 No. 25 [*1]In the Matter of P.C., Respondent, v Stony Brook University, et al., Appellants. Elizabeth A. Brody, for appellants. Alexander Klein, for respondent. CANNATARO, J. Petitioner, a student at respondent Stony Brook University (the University), commenced this CPLR article 78 proceeding challenging the determination that he violated the University's Code of Student Responsibility by committing sexual misconduct against another student. We hold that the determination at issue is supported by substantial evidence and therefore reverse the order of the Appellate Division. I. In September 2019, following a report indicating that petitioner, P.C., had engaged in behavior that violated the University's sexual misconduct policy, the University commenced an investigation. The other student involved, S.G., provided a written statement to the investigator in which she recounted the details of their encounter. P.C. declined to meet with the University's investigator. Following the investigation, P.C. was charged with violating three provisions of the Code of Student Responsibility relating to sexual misconduct, namely, sexual harassment, nonconsensual sexual contact and nonconsensual sexual intercourse and/or penetration. The Notice of Charges detailed the allegations lodged against P.C., that he "engaged in sexual contact with a female student while she was incapacitated due to alcohol and unable to give consent," and listed specific behaviors, including choking S.G. during sexual intercourse in the woods and having sexual intercourse in S.G.'s vehicle. The Notice also set forth in full the text of the Code provisions P.C. was alleged to have violated. As relevant here, the definition of sexual harassment encompasses unwelcome sexual [*2]advances and physical conduct of a sexual nature, including sexual violence (Code of Student Responsibility § VII.C.6.a). Nonconsensual sexual contact includes "any contact of a sexual nature which is unwanted or unwelcome" (Code of Student Responsibility § VII.C.6.b) and nonconsensual sexual intercourse is "any sexual penetration or intercourse that is unwanted or unwelcome" (Code of Student Responsibility § VII.C.6.c). II. A hearing was held before a Review Panel composed of faculty and staff members from the University. P.C. was represented by counsel. The University's investigator placed a summary of the investigation on the record and S.G. gave a statement consistent with her prior written statement. With respect to the choking allegation, S.G. testified that she had been "black[ing] out," but "became present in the moment because of how aggressive [P.C.] was being, how I felt like I couldn't breathe and tried to get his hands off my throat. He wasn't budging and I don't know what happen[ed] after that because I blacked out again." With respect to the sexual intercourse in her car, S.G. stated that she did not recall much of what happened, but remembered "dreaming as if [she] were asleep" and, when she "woke up," she "remember[ed] panicking, asking [P.C.] if I passed out" and that he initially said no, but then said she was "only out for a moment." She also recalled swiftly terminating the encounter, returning to her dorm and crying on the phone with her friends, telling them that she "woke up and it was still happening. He didn't stop." Video surveillance footage showing the two walking together around campus at various points in the evening was played during the cross examination of S.G. P.C. provided a brief opening statement denying that he engaged in sexual conduct with S.G. while she was incapacitated due to alcohol and unable to consent. He generally argued that S.G. was not credible, asserting that the surveillance footage showing the two walking together around campus at various points in the evening belied any claim of inability to consent due to incapacitation by alcohol. He also argued that the allegation that she was violently choked should not be believed, given that there were no marks on her neck. P.C. confirmed that he was familiar with the definition of affirmative consent set forth in the Code of Student Responsibility. P.C. then declined to answer most of the questions asked by the hearing officer on the advice of counsel, including whether he could identify actions or words by S.G. during the sexual interactions that constituted affirmative consent. No other testimony was taken, but text messages exchanged between P.C. and another individual—a mutual friend who had introduced P.C. and S.G. that evening and had elicited a promise from P.C. that he would not have sex with S.G.—were introduced into evidence. In the messages, P.C. admitted he had sex with S.G., stating "I made my choice, and I'm sorry, and I know I f***ed up, and I won't sugar coat that." P.C. also acknowledged that he "did something terrible, and I don't know how to say I'm sorry, but I am." In explaining why he had sex with S.G., he said "I was drunk and horny and let my monkey brain have fun in the moment despite the obvious long-term outcome. What I'm saying is that if I had been sober, I would've been thinking more straight and I wouldn't have hurt her nor broken your trust." The Review Panel found P.C. responsible for violating the charged provisions of the Code of Student Responsibility by a preponderance of the evidence at the hearing. In support of its determination, the Review Panel pointed to S.G.'s testimony that P.C. engaged in conduct that amounted to unwelcome sexual advances, unwelcome sexual contact and unwelcome sexual intercourse, primarily that S.G. did not want P.C. to choke her during sex and that he admitted to her that she was briefly unconscious while they were having sex in the car. The Panel also cited to P.C.'s text messages, in which he acknowledged engaging in sexual intercourse with the victim and stated that he "f***ed up." The Review Panel stated that it had considered all available information and determined that, regardless of whether S.G. was incapacitated by alcohol, the evidence supported the conclusion that P.C. was responsible for the charged misconduct. The Panel imposed a penalty of suspension from the University. P.C. administratively appealed the determination, arguing that the violations of the Code of Student Responsibility were not established by a preponderance of the evidence. Despite his acknowledgement that the Review Panel did not base its determination on the question of S.G.'s inability to consent due to intoxication, P.C. nonetheless devoted a significant portion of his argument to evidence that purportedly negated any claim that S.G. was incapacitated by alcohol. He further posited that the evidence introduced at the hearing was sufficient to establish affirmative consent, citing S.G.'s statements relating to their consensual sexual activity that night. Finally, he argued that the Review Panel improperly held his decision to remain silent against him and improperly referenced his inability or unwillingness to identify evidence establishing affirmative consent, in violation of the presumption of non-responsibility contained in the Student Code. The Appeals Committee found "no grounds upon which to alter the Review Panel's determination" and upheld the disciplinary penalty. The Committee rejected the argument that S.G. was not credible. In addition, the Committee found that the evidence supported the Review Panel's findings of responsibility on all three charges based on a preponderance of the evidence. The Committee explained that, although P.C. was permitted to decline to answer questions put to him at the hearing, the Review Panel was constrained to consider only the evidence in the record and that his decision not to answer questions limited the evidence that could be considered. III. Petitioner commenced this CPLR article 78 proceeding against respondents [FN1] seeking to vacate the Appeals Committee's determination, asserting that it lacked substantial evidence and that it was arbitrary and capricious and made pursuant to an error of law due to the University's failure to follow its own rules for disciplinary proceedings. In particular, he asserted that the University did not adhere to the standard requiring that misconduct be established by a preponderance of the evidence and that it failed to accord him a "presumption of innocence." [FN2] Upon transfer from Supreme Court pursuant to CPLR 7804 (g), a majority of the Appellate Division granted the petition, annulled the Appeals Committee's determination, dismissed the charges and directed the University to expunge the matter from petitioner's academic record ( 221 AD3d 686 [2d Dept 2023]). Since the University Review Panel made no determination that S.G. was unable to consent as a result of incapacitation caused by intoxication, the Court deemed the only question before it to be whether substantial evidence supported the conclusion that S.G. did not otherwise consent to the sexual activity. The majority determined that substantial evidence was lacking to support that conclusion, specifically referencing S.G.'s written statement that she consented to sexual activities earlier in the evening. In addition, the majority found that reliance on P.C.'s decision not to answer certain questions violated the presumption of non-responsibility contained in the Code of Student Responsibility. Two Justices dissented and would have confirmed the determination, denied the petition and dismissed the proceeding.
